title: Mapped Types
summary: Build one type from the keys of another with mapped types, add or remove readonly and optional, and rename or drop keys with as.
intro: The utility types from the last lesson aren't special. `Partial`, `Required`, `Readonly`, `Pick`, and `Record` are short declarations in TypeScript's own library, and each one is a mapped type: a type that goes through the keys of another type and decides what each key becomes. In this lesson you write your own, so a form's errors, its validators, a draft you fill in step by step, and a set of event handlers all follow the one type they describe.

steps.title: Mapping over keys

examples.title: Feature flags per plan
examples.prompt: Map every feature to an on or off switch, and list the features each plan turns on.
examples.output:
free: darkMode, search
pro: darkMode, search, csvExport

examples.title: A validator per field
examples.prompt: Give every field of a contact form its own validator, and run them all in a loop over a list of the form's keys.
examples.output:
ok
name is required, email needs an @, message is too short
examples.explanation:
`Validators<ContactForm>` gives each key a function that takes that key's own type, `T[K]`. Every field here is a `string`, so each `value` is a string. A `guests: number` field would get a validator that takes a `number`.

The loop needs the form's keys. `Object.keys(form)` would give a `string[]`, not a list of the form's keys, because an object can hold more keys than its type lists: thanks to structural typing, a bigger object fits a smaller type. Indexing `validators` with a plain `string` doesn't compile. So keep the keys you want in a list: `as const` keeps each one as a literal, and `satisfies readonly (keyof ContactForm)[]` checks that each is a real key, so a typo like `"emial"` is an error. It doesn't check that the list has every key, so keep it next to the type.

examples.title: Errors only where they apply
examples.prompt: Validate a profile, and return an object with a message only for the fields that need one.
examples.output:
{}
{"username":"must be at least 3 characters","website":"must start with https://"}
examples.explanation: The `?` after the brackets makes every key optional, and every key holds a `string`, whatever the field itself holds. So `errors` starts empty and gets one message per broken rule. A key you never set doesn't exist, which is why the valid profile prints `{}` and the JSON skips the fields without an error. The type still knows the form: `errors.email = "..."` is TS2339, because a profile has no `email`. And with this course's `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, `errors.bio = undefined` is an error too, so a field with no error always looks the same: the key is missing.

practice.title: Form errors
practice.prompt:
Write an errors type that works for any form, then use it to validate signup forms.

1. Make `FieldErrors<T>` a mapped type over the keys of `T`, where every key is optional and holds a `string`.
2. Make `validate` add an error for each rule the form breaks: an `email` without an `@` gets `must contain @`, a `password` shorter than 8 characters gets `must be at least 8 characters`, and an `age` under 13 gets `must be at least 13`.
3. Check the rules in that order, so the keys print in that order. The loop that prints each form's errors as JSON is done.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests use `FieldErrors`, `SignupForm`, and `validate`.

Expected output:

```text
{}
{"email":"must contain @","age":"must be at least 13"}
```

typeTests.imports: import { validate, type FieldErrors, type SignupForm } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: accepts a form with no errors
rejects a field the form doesn't have
holds a message, not the field's value
works for any form
cases.code: const e: FieldErrors<{ city: string }> = { city: "is required" };

cases.name: returns the errors of a signup form
cases.code: const e: FieldErrors<SignupForm> = validate({ email: "a@b.c", password: "12345678", age: 20 });

hints: `FieldErrors` in the third example builds the same type for a profile form.
`[K in keyof T]?: string` gives every key of `T` an optional string. Then write one `if` per rule in `validate`.
`export type FieldErrors<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: string };` and, for the first rule, `if (!form.email.includes("@")) { errors.email = "must contain @"; }`

steps.title: Adding and removing modifiers

examples.title: Your own Partial
examples.prompt: Write Partial yourself, then use it for patches the same way as the built-in.
examples.explanation: `MyPartial` copies every key of `User` with its type, `T[K]`, and the `?` makes each one optional. The two bubbles are identical because the library declares `Partial` as this same mapped type. That's also why `update` accepts `newEmail`, a value typed with the built-in: TypeScript compares shapes, not names. Since `+` is the default, `+?` means the same as `?`, and you'll rarely see it written out.

examples.title: A builder with Mutable
examples.prompt: Fill in a read-only invoice step by step inside a builder, then hand out the finished invoice as read-only.
examples.explanation: Inside `buildInvoice`, `Mutable<Invoice>` removes `readonly` from all three keys, so the loop can reassign `lines` and add to `totalCents`. The function returns it as an `Invoice`, so every caller gets the read-only version, and `invoice.totalCents = 0` after the call is TS2540. `-readonly` only reaches the top level: `lines` is still a `readonly string[]`, so `invoice.lines.push(...)` fails even inside the builder, which is why the loop builds a new array. Like `Readonly`, `Mutable` only changes what `tsc` allows. Nothing is frozen or unfrozen while the program runs.

examples.title: Options with every key set
examples.prompt: Resolve optional retry options against defaults, so the code after it reads every option without a fallback.
examples.output:
{"retries":5,"delayMs":500,"verbose":false}
Waits up to 2500 ms in all
examples.explanation: `-?` removes the question mark from every key, so `Concrete<RetryOptions>` is the same type as `Required<RetryOptions>`. `DEFAULTS` must give all three options a value, or it doesn't compile. In `resolve`, the spread copies the defaults, then the options the caller passed. With `exactOptionalPropertyTypes`, a caller can't pass `retries: undefined`, so nothing in `options` can blank out a default. After `resolve`, `options.retries * options.delayMs` needs no `??`, because both are plain numbers, as the bubble on `total` shows.

practice.title: Draft to final
practice.prompt:
Build an article as a draft, one field at a time, and turn it into a finished article once it has what it needs.

1. Make `Draft<T>` a mapped type over the keys of `T` that removes `readonly` and makes every key optional.
2. Make `finalize` return `null` when the draft has no `id` or no `title`, else an `Article` with all of the draft's fields.
3. After the first print, set the draft's `id` to `"a1"` and its `tags` to `["typescript", "types"]`, then print `show(finalize(draft))` again.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests use `Article`, `Draft`, and `finalize`.

Expected output:

```text
not ready
a1: Mapped types [typescript, types]
```

tests.output:
not ready
a1: Mapped types [typescript, types]

typeTests.imports: import { finalize, type Article, type Draft } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: lets you set the id later
keeps the type of each field
keeps a finished article's id read-only
finalizes a draft with an id and a title
cases.code: const a: Article | null = finalize({ id: "a1", title: "Types" });

hints: `Mutable` in the second example removes `readonly`, and `MyPartial` in the first adds `?`. `Draft` does both in one mapped type.
Write `-readonly` before the brackets and `?` after them. In `finalize`, return `null` first when `d.id` or `d.title` is `undefined`.
`export type Draft<T> = { -readonly [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };` and, after the check, `return { ...d, id: d.id, title: d.title };`

steps.title: Renaming keys with as

examples.title: Getter methods
examples.prompt: Derive an account's getter methods from its fields, and build an object that has exactly those methods.
examples.explanation: For each key, `as` builds a new name: `owner` becomes `getOwner`, and `balanceCents` becomes `getBalanceCents`. The value type `() => T[K]` makes each one a function that returns the field's type, so `getBalanceCents()` returns a `number`. The return type holds `accountGetters` to exactly these names. Leave one out, and `tsc` reports it missing (TS2741). Misspell one, and the excess property check reports it (TS2353). Add a field to `Account`, and the function stops compiling until it has a getter for the new field.

examples.title: Only the text fields
examples.prompt: Keep only the string fields of a product type, and use their names to search products by text.
examples.output:
Blue mug, Tall mug
Green tea

examples.title: Handlers for every event
examples.prompt: Turn a map of upload events into handler names, and check an object of handlers against it with satisfies.
examples.explanation: `Handlers<UploadEvents>` turns each event name into an `on` name, and each handler takes its event's payload, `E[K]`. `satisfies` checks the object against that type: every handler must be there, and a name the type doesn't have, like a misspelled `onFinish`, is an error. It also gives each `e` its type from its event, so `e.percent` needs no annotation. And since `satisfies` keeps the object's own type, the calls know exactly which handlers exist.

practice.title: Cart handlers
practice.prompt:
Derive the handler names for a cart's events, write one handler per event, and call each one once.

1. Make `Handlers<E>` a mapped type that renames each key of `E` to `on` plus the key with a capital first letter (`added` becomes `onAdded`), and gives it a function that takes that event's payload and returns `void`.
2. Write `handlers`, checked with `satisfies Handlers<CartEvents>`: `onAdded` prints `Added <sku>`, `onRemoved` prints `Removed <sku>`, and `onCleared` prints `Cart cleared at <at>`.
3. Call `onAdded` with the sku `MUG-01`, `onRemoved` with the sku `TEA-02`, and `onCleared` with the time `2026-10-01T09:00:00Z`, in that order.
4. Keep `export`: hidden type tests use `CartEvents`, `Handlers`, and `handlers`.

Expected output:

```text
Added MUG-01
Removed TEA-02
Cart cleared at 2026-10-01T09:00:00Z
```

tests.output:
Added MUG-01
Removed TEA-02
Cart cleared at 2026-10-01T09:00:00Z

typeTests.imports: import { handlers, type CartEvents, type Handlers } from "./main.ts";

cases.name: needs a handler for every event
rejects a handler for an event that doesn't exist
cases.code: const h: Handlers<CartEvents> = { onAdded: () => {}, onRemoved: () => {}, onCleared: () => {}, onSaved: () => {} };

cases.name: gives each handler its own payload
works for any map of events
cases.code: const h: Handlers<{ saved: { id: number } }> = { onSaved: (e) => console.log(e.id) };

hints: `Handlers` in the third example is the same type, written for upload events. Only the events differ.
After `as`, the new name is a template literal type: `on` followed by `${Capitalize<string & K>}`, all inside backticks. Each handler's parameter is `E[K]`.
Each handler is an arrow that prints one line, like `onAdded: (e) => console.log(...)`. `satisfies` gives `e` its payload type, so it needs no annotation.

recap:
- `{ [K in keyof T]: X }` builds a type with the keys of `T`, and `T[K]` is the type each key held in `T`.
- `readonly` before the brackets and `?` after them change every key at once, and a `-` in front removes them. `Partial`, `Required`, and `Readonly` are written exactly this way.
- `as` after the key renames it. A template literal type with `${Capitalize<string & K>}` builds a new name from the old one, and a key renamed to `never` is dropped.
- `Object.keys` returns `string[]`, because an object can hold more keys than its type lists. Loop over an `as const` list of keys, checked with `satisfies readonly (keyof T)[]`, instead.
- Mapped types follow the type they map: add a key, and every type built from it gains the key.
